utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please be seated. Usher, please have the witness brought in. (The accused/witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Good afternoon to the interpreters, to the court stenographers. I see that they are here again. Also, good afternoon to counsel for Prosecution and the Defence, and good afternoon to the witness. This is a public hearing. Let me remind those people who are in the public gallery that in the trial which is being conducted by the Office of the Prosecutor against General Blaskic, the accused chose to testify. Like any witness, he is under oath. This is now the cross-examination of General Blaskic. I would like to recall, for reasons that all of you working in the Tribunal know, and given certain solemn ceremonies that are taking place at the Peace Palace, after some hesitation, the Judges have chosen for a minimal type of formula both to show that they are participating in an important event a century ago, that is an advance in International Humanitarian Law which interests all of us and which marks the progress of civilisation, and not to disturb the conduct of our hearings, because our most important work is to render tribute to International Law and in doing so to devote ourselves primarily to the trial. In agreement with my colleagues, as I always wish to work, with their agreement we decided that we would not have a hearing tomorrow morning but only tomorrow afternoon, and we will resume our hearings but we will begin at 2.00, in the beginning of the afternoon, and we will stop at 5.30. So that tomorrow afternoon the registrar has to note that there will be a hearing from 2.00 until 5.30. We don't have a great deal of time. Let me remind the Prosecutor about the time constraints, and remind the witness as well so he can answer as concisely as possible those questions that have been asked him -- that he's been asked by the Prosecutor. Mr. Prosecutor, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good afternoon, Mr. President, Your Honours, Counsel. Good afternoon, General.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good day.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Cross-examined by Mr. Kehoe:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, let us turn our attention back to Prosecutor's Exhibit 678. General, 678 is the exhibit that we spoke about at the end of last week concerning the burned houses in the Busovaca municipality in the area under HVO control, and of the 112 buildings damaged, we noted in paragraph 1, 53 were burned down. Now, General, both during your time in Kiseljak and after you returned to Vitez on the 3rd of March, you were aware of crimes committed by HVO troops in Busovaca, in the Busovaca municipality, were you not?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: As regards this document 678, it is only a partial document that was used for the work of the joint commission. As for the report --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Excuse me, General, that's not my question. My question for you is: Were you made aware or were you aware of crimes committed by HVO troops in the Busovaca municipality during January and February of 1993? Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: As regards the report pertaining to the crime that was committed by individuals from the HVO when they took two prisoners to dig trenches, I was informed about that. I asked for an investigation to be carried out. The investigation was carried out and the criminals were prosecuted by the district military court in Travnik whose seat was in Vitez. I asked for an investigation to be carried out about each and every individual crime that I heard about through reports. I only know about the crimes that I heard about through the reports of the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I think that we've heard that. Let's move to the next question, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, what were these crimes that you heard about that were committed by HVO troops?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: It was the crime of taking two prisoners or, rather, taking them out of the district military prison by force to dig trenches and then these two prisoners were killed. This was done by a group of persons who were identified and then criminally prosecuted before the district military court in Travnik. The seat of the court was then in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that the only crime that you were made aware of?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I was informed about that crime, and I was informed about the crimes that were committed in Lasva, in the village of Dusina, in Visnjica. Then --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Excuse me, General. If we want to clarify this, please, we are talking about crimes committed by HVO troops in the Busovaca municipality. Other than the two individuals that you allege were convicted for forcing Muslims to trench dig, what other crimes by HVO troops were you made aware of that were committed in the Busovaca municipality?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I do not remember having received any other information related to crimes committed by members of the HVO. As regards this document, I already said that this was a partial document, document 678, because a comprehensive document shows that there was house burning on both sides. Actually, at a ratio 3 to 1, Croatian houses compared to Muslims houses that were burned down.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, General, of the 53 houses that were burnt down and the 112 buildings that were damaged as we see in 678, did you investigate the method and means in which those houses were damaged and destroyed, given that they were in HVO controlled areas or did you just disregard this?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I did not disregard a single report, but I should clarify how these reports were processed by the joint commission which was set up in order to take care of everything that had happened as a result of the conflict in Busovaca and Kiseljak municipalities, that is to say, the joint commission collected comprehensive reports and then it informed me about this as well as the commander of the 3rd Corps. On the basis of the conclusions that were reached at meetings, joint orders were passed as well forbidding the burning of buildings and other non-military conduct. So over a longer period of time, this was dictated by the chief of the European Monitoring Mission, Mr. Thebault, and most things were done under the mandate of the European Monitoring Mission within this joint commission.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, listen to me very clearly. What HVO soldiers were disciplined, arrested, or convicted for burning Muslim houses in the Busovaca municipality in January and February of 1993?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: As regards disciplinary action, I already said that house burning is a criminal offence. Information reached the commander, then a criminal report was filed on that kind of offence. So it is not disciplinary action that could be taken against the same soldier against whom criminal proceedings were investigated against, that is to say, criminal proceedings were initiated at the district military court in Travnik. This court was not under my jurisdiction and I did not have the right to carry out this kind of prosecution. According to the law on criminal procedure, I did not have jurisdiction over the criminal procedure and investigation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, my question is very simple. What information came to your attention about HVO soldiers burning down houses in Busovaca? What information came to your attention?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: For a longer period of time, from January almost until March, I did not receive any information because I was isolated and cut off, that is to say, I spent that time in Kiseljak. I only got information from the joint commission, that commission which was chaired by Mr. Dzemo Merdan and by Mr. Franjo Nakic. The burning of houses is a criminal offence, and I have no power or control over --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Excuse me, General. Excuse me, General. The question is: What information came to your attention? You got back to Vitez on 3 March, 1993. After you got back to Vitez on 3 March, 1993, what information came to your attention about HVO soldiers burning houses in the Busovaca municipality in January and February of 1993?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: At that time I did not receive any information, but only at the next meeting. I think it was in March 1993, in Zenica. This was a joint meeting between myself and the commander of the 3rd Corps. At that meeting, in the presence of Mr. Thebault, a report was submitted on buildings that were burned down. This was a joint report, and at these meetings we worked in accordance with the conclusions of the chairman of this meeting, that is to say, Mr. Thebault.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, what individuals in the HVO were responsible for these burnings? If you do not understand the question, General, I will rephrase the question. But I'm looking for individuals within the HVO responsible for these burnings based on the information you received.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, Mr. Kehoe is prefacing his questions with "Listen to me very carefully," and "You're not answering the question," and so forth. He's asking different questions. He's trying to create the impression that he's asking the same question and not getting an answer, but if you look at the transcript over the last three or four or five questions, he's changing the question every time but making these speeches about how he's unhappy and, "Oh, won't the witness listen to the question," et cetera. He should ask questions and keep his comments to himself, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Would you like to make a comment, Mr. Kehoe, about what Mr. Hayman has just said?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I think Mr. President and Your Honours have seen the reluctance with which the witness wants to answer a direct question. This has been going on for weeks with the witness being reluctant to answer a direct question not only from the Prosecutor but also from Your Honours. In order to cut short that, given the amount of time that the witness wants to waste during the answering of those questions, I want to make those questions very clear and very explicit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Let me take your place, Mr. Prosecutor. I was wondering, General Blaskic, the question that you were asked for the third time, that is, whether you were aware of HVO soldiers who had been sanctioned or punished for those crimes, you at one point said that it was a procedure for the court, and at the proper time we will see whether in wartime an ordinary law court can judge that type of case. You also said most recently that you held a meeting with Mr. Thebault. I didn't change my question. I simply want to know whether HVO soldiers were punished, whether they were sanctioned. I assume that there would be disciplinary sanctions. Answer very quickly, please. A crime is committed -- quickly, please, succinctly; otherwise I'm going to stop you -- were there disciplinary measures taken as a result? I wanted to remind you, Mr. Hayman, that ordinarily the witness is alone when he has to answer. Let me remind you of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, but you're pressing him to answer quickly, quickly, quickly. He doesn't have the translation yet, and it is difficult because Your Honour speaks very rapidly too. I'm hearing it in English and it is difficult. In his language, I'm sure it's difficult too, so please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, you're right, Mr. Hayman. Excuse me. I will try to reformulate my question. When you were asked whether HVO soldiers were punished in Busovaca, I wanted to ask you only whether they were sanctioned by the court, and at the same time, were they the subject of disciplinary measures that were taken?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Mr. President, the practice in the HVO was the following: If a soldier commits a crime, then a criminal report is filed against him to the district military court, and it is not disciplinary action that follows but criminal prosecution of that person. The military district prosecutor and the district military court are in charge of this criminal procedure against a soldier, but if a disciplinary infraction is committed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I hate to interrupt you, General Blaskic, but you've said that several times, and we have the weakness of knowing that now, but that is not my question. You, as the commander, did you take any disciplinary measures? For example, they would not be allowed to return to the HVO.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I received a report that a soldier, given his name and surname, committed a disciplinary infraction, then I would certainly take care of that particular case, and I would certainly impose a disciplinary action.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I'm speaking to you about crimes, burned houses. When an HVO soldier -- let me speak slowly -- is suspected of having committed a war crime, at the same time, did you begin a disciplinary procedure?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. A criminal procedure is initiated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. Therefore, at that point, you keep the soldier as one of your military personnel?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. The soldier is placed under criminal investigation, he is detained, and an investigation is carried out against him, but it is the district military prosecutor who is in charge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We've got to where we wanted to get. As a commander in the HVO, did your brigade commanders, and specifically in Busovaca, did they say that "Starting from such and such a day, we have ten HVO members who, for alleged crimes, have been brought to the district military court, and for the time being, they are no longer part of the HVO army"? Did you have information in that respect?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I did have information in this respect for this case related to the killing of prisoners of war who were digging trenches, that is to say, that these soldiers were sent away from the unit, they were detained, and a criminal prosecution was initiated against them. They were no longer members of the HVO units.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: For all the crimes in Busovaca, did you have any other information which you might be able to give to your Defence attorneys? It's important to know because you're the one who is saying so.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Mr. President, I did not have the right to supervise the work of the district military court; however, specifically --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I'm not talking about the military court's work, General Blaskic. Please listen; try to focus. I'm asking you, among the members who were there, with someone who was being brought before the military trial because of a complaint, you're saying that ipso facto he would no longer be counted among the HVO military personnel; is that correct? Did the Busovaca commander tell you, "Starting tomorrow, there are ten HVO soldiers who will no longer be part of the HVO army because they are being tried by the military court. They are being prosecuted." That's my question. It's very simple.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, he did inform me. I said about this concrete example of the killing of prisoners of war, that is to say, that the suspects were sent away from HVO ranks, that they were detained --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: That one case then. There was only that one case?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I had information about that case. During the conflict, I was isolated in Kiseljak. I did not receive all information from units. They arrived to headquarters in Vitez. I received very little information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: You are a general and a commander in chief who was very poorly informed. At least that's all we can see. Please continue, Mr. Prosecutor. You're missing a lot of information. That's what can be said. That's the answer that would have been sufficient to give. Now, Mr. Prosecutor, please change the subject area. We're starting with the idea that the general, who was a colonel at the time, was badly informed about what was going on in Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us turn to the time when you were back in Vitez, and you got back on the 3rd of March, and you told us, in response to questions by my colleague, that you then took steps to fight criminals and criminal activity in the Central Bosnia Operative Zone; do you recall that testimony?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What types of crimes were you trying to stop?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: All forms of criminal behaviour on the part of HVO members, that is to say, any activity that constituted a crime, regardless of whether this was looting, robbery, highway robbery, the burning of buildings, any form of criminal activity.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you learn that this criminal activity was going on? Was it a constant type of activity? Was it intermittent?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: There were such activities in different periods of time depending on the situation, on the military situation. Especially when larger groups of refugees would come in, for example, from Jajce, then there were more criminals on the ground as well. However, the greatest problem was to establish, under those circumstances, who the protagonists of crime were, whether it was civilians or soldiers, because the same person would play the role of a soldier from one to seven days, and then after that, for 21 days, he would be a civilian, this person, and live in a home with his family. So it was very difficult to establish whether the perpetrator of the crime was a soldier or a civilian, especially because criminal offences were usually committed at night and in conditions when it was very difficult to discover this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, do you believe that you did everything in your power to stop this criminal activity?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. I'm deeply convinced that I did absolutely everything that was within my power to stop this, and I also tried to extend my command responsibilities because I kept insisting on changing the structure of the HVO. Because I said that the military police was an instrument of command and control but also an important instrument of security which was not under my command, which certainly made it more difficult to prevent violence, terror, and crime within my zone of responsibility. So we tried for a longer period of time to eliminate the protagonists of unrest and crime in the HVO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What steps did you take to eliminate these criminals within the HVO when you came back in March of 1993?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I demanded from my immediate subordinates to identify all the protagonists of destructive behaviour and criminal behaviour, then to make out lists of such persons, to try to disarm them, and also take their war assignments way from them, that is to say, that the competent civilian authorities give such persons a different war duty, that it be work duty rather than military duty, so that at least formally, they would be prevented from carrying weapons and keeping military equipment and other means in their hands which made them even more powerful. So practically in every brigade, we managed to identify lists with the protagonists of such criminal behaviour. In addition to this, I tried to change the structure within the organisation of the military police. The civilian authorities also passed decisions on curfew in order to restrict the possibility of committing violence against all citizens and improving law and order within this area that was within the zone of responsibility of Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, tell us about these criminal groups that you discussed on direct examination. What were the names of these criminal groups?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: These were groups in the Lasva River Valley, practically in every municipality, and they were organised round individuals, round their leaders. Most often, individuals from these groups were infiltrated into HVO units as well. There were different groups, and usually they were called by the name of their leader, Poskoci, Celavi, and they were readily recognisable by their hairstyles. They had short haircuts, and they were well-armed, well-equipped, and they had high quality weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, was the Vitezovi one of these groups?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: There were individuals within the Vitezovi who took part in such groups, but the whole unit had a total of about 120 soldiers, and it's not that the entire unit belonged to this kind of a group. However, the Vitezovi had a high degree of autonomy and, otherwise, a high degree of independence as well. One could not say, though, that all of them were in a criminal group but there were individuals of this nature in Vitezovi as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So in addition to having, in your view, a high degree of autonomy, there were criminals within the Vitezovi as well; is that right?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, there were persons who had a criminal record from the former structure, before they belonged to the HOS. They were established from three different municipalities, and most of them were young men from Vitez who only changed their name from the HOS into the special purpose unit Vitezovi, and they had a high degree of autonomy. However, it is certain that the whole unit was not a criminal one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, you told us during your direct examination, on page 18085, that on the 15th of November General Merdan was arrested and taken into custody by the Vitezovi. That is on the page, as I noted, 18085. On 18095 you told us that on the 2nd of January, in the town of Vitez, opening of fire as well as active provocation by the special purpose unit Vitezovi in the course of the 2nd of January. You also told us, page 18267, that General Merdan informed you that the Vitezovi were dealing with problems in the individual villages by using ultimatums and he had in mind Bosnian Muslim villages. This is the same group that is controlled by Darko Kraljevic, who, in response to Judge Rodrigues's question on page 19510, you noted that: "The commander of the Vitezovi had a selective approach to my orders, so if he considered or if his position coincided with the duties that I assigned to him, then he would carry them out. If not, then he would not carry them out or he would carry them out as he saw fit." Now, that's one in the same group that contains these criminal -- well, some criminal elements that you wanted to remove from Central Bosnia; is that right?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I didn't understand the last question. I don't know what it pertains to. I tried to remove him? Who is he? Who is the person I'm trying to remove from Central Bosnia, or perhaps the interpretation was wrong.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I apologise. You wanted to remove the Vitezovi as an independent unit from Central Bosnia; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. I asked the members of the joint command to do that. I wanted this unit to be dislocated from Central Bosnia. I wanted it to be in Mostar where its direct command and headquarters were. But in relation to the abduction of Dzemo Merdan, I would like to say a few words. It is true that this happened. However, I found out about the reason only later, because there were mutual arrests between the Vitezovi and the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and the commander tried to free them, et cetera, et cetera. As for resolving the problem of the ultimatum, I think it is very important to understand that I asked Dzemo Merdan to tell me in which villages the Vitezovi were presenting ultimatums and solving problems by ultimatums, and Mr. Dzemo Merdan didn't give an answer, any answer, to that. He didn't say which villages this concerned or where this was happening. So I thought that this claim was made at this meeting but it was unspecified.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, the bottom line with the Vitezovi is, according to your testimony, there were criminals within the Vitezovi and the Vitezovi and its commander essentially did what they wanted; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Reading document 250 that I read through several days ago, I saw that they did certain operations on command, but I had no insight into the orders they were receiving, and I thought they were doing this arbitrarily, on their own, or following the wishes of their commander. There were situations where they took independent decisions, the commanders of the Vitezovi that is, and sometimes they were following orders from their superiors. However, in both cases, in both situations, I was not informed about their actions. So what I found very difficult is I was not able to establish control over their activities, in fact, and this made it very difficult for me to operate in the Central Bosnia area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us turn to the military police, and in response to this question and answer by Mr. Nobilo at 18405 at line 2, Mr. Nobilo notes that: "Q On 24 March --" And that's 24 March, 1993, General. "Q On 24 March there was something relative to the military police. You had a discussion with the deputy commander. If you can tell us now so that we don't have to repeat it every day, because now we will encounter this more frequently, what was the situation like in the military police with respect to crime? A Within the military police, there was some perpetrators of criminal acts. In other words, individuals who had previous criminal records, and on several occasions, I insisted that measures against such individuals be taken as part of the reorganisation of the military police." Now, General, as of -- do I have the wrong page, counsel?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I believe that's correct, counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Wrong transcript, counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Then it's either 18394 -- top of the page.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, as of the 24th of March, you were aware of criminals within the military police; is that right?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I knew that as of that date there were indeed individuals who had criminal records and who had committed certain crimes. That is why I demanded that corresponding measures be taken against them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Answer the question, General. There is no need -- well, you already said that starting the 24th of March there were individuals with criminal records. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Approximately how many individuals within the military police had criminal records? Would it be in excess of 100 or in excess of 200? How many?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Approximately, taking the whole of the 4th Battalion, about 100 individuals for which I sought measures to be taken against them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What types of crimes that you were informed had that these members of the military police committed?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I did not receive specific information as to the types of crimes committed. What I did receive was information that they were individuals with criminal records, that is to say, individuals who had previous criminal records before the war broke out, and that these criminal records were kept as records -- indeed are kept by the police station in the towns and areas.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, in addition to the criminal records that these individuals had, you were also informed of such things as abuse of prisoners in Kaonik camp, which came after your discussion with Mr. Aleksovski, the warden of the prison, and that conversation took place on the 25th of March, 1993, is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That, I believe, is at 18398, counsel, top of the page, lines 3 through 6.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I can read it to you, General, if you see fit. "Q Did he ..." Speaking of Aleksovski. "... have any complaints about the military police? A Yes. He also had certain complaints about the behaviour of individual members of the military police and their treatment of detainees and, also, their treatment of the guards at the district military police prison." So you had that information as well.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I received that information at the meeting, from the warden, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did information about the military police abusing detainees, and the guards -- you knew that there were approximately 100 with criminal records in the military police -- what other crimes were you informed that the military police were committing in Central Bosnia while you were under command? For clarity's sake, if I might just shorten it, prior to Ahmici. Prior to the 16th of April.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I did not have information that the members of the military police had perpetrated war crimes before that, before the events in Ahmici. I did not have any information of that kind, not for any of the members of the military police. I spoke about the criminal records that existed before the war broke out, for those individuals whom I -- because I considered these individuals could not be members of the military police if they had previous criminal records.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, General, let us turn to Tvrtko, the special purpose unit Tvrtko. What was the status of the members of the Tvrtko? Did they also contain individuals with criminal records in their ranks?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I did not have any data on them, that is to say, whether there were individuals with criminal records. I don't remember receiving any information of that nature.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, there was another group that was controlled by an individual by the name of Zuti which Mr. Nobilo described in page 19612 as "Mafioso boss," and I quote. Tell us a little bit about Zuti and his criminal activities.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, he was within the composition of the military police unit when the military police was organised to begin with. He was an influential individual in the region and, for the most part, crime groups would refer to him during their operations. As I say, he was a mighty individual, a powerful individual, and members of the UNPROFOR would contact him as well. I think I mentioned that in the course of my testimony previously. There were groups from different local communities, municipalities, Travnik, Novi Travnik, and Vitez, and they would refer to authorisation from Zuti, although, there was little data on his personal influence and personal activities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us about the information that you received about the crimes that Zuti was committing. What crimes was Zuti and his Mafia group committing?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Most frequently it was looting and gaining material, wealth, and black marketeering. Black marketeering under wartime conditions. That would be the best term to use. The looting of convoys, seizing various goods from the convoy, high-profit goods, cigarettes, coffee, alcoholic beverages, and the individuals would refer to his name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, let us turn to a few of those instances, and let me turn first to Defence Exhibit 213. Now, General, this is a Defence document concerning the incident where one of Zuti's gang, Ferdo Gazibaric, was brought in for questioning by the military police. Then Zuti, Zarko Andric, and other individuals from Vitezovi and Tvrtko II broke him out of the gaol; is that right?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. I was in Kiseljak when the incident occurred.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The person who wrote this is Pasko Ljubicic, the commander of the 4th Military Police Battalion; correct?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. Pasko Ljubicic wrote the report to his superiors, Valentin Coric and to the SIS head Ivica Lucic in person, but I did not receive this document and it wasn't addressed to me either.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The other person that signs this document is Miso Mijic, a commander of SIS; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Miso Mijic, I don't know what his functions in SIS were apart from the fact that sometime from April he was the head of the SIS centre. He has signed himself here as official -- SIS official for the Central Bosnia Operative Zone. Perhaps that is within the structure, although I don't know the structure but I do know that he was head of SIS at one point.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were made aware of these events that were taking place in Vitez and in Busovaca while you were in Kiseljak, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. By telephone, the ordinary type of civilian telephone, I was informed about the events and I had the opportunity of talking to both the participants, that is to say, with Pasko Ljubicic, who informed me about it, and with Zuti, who was next to Pasko in the same office. The events were also witnessed by a major belonging to UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you returned to Vitez on the 3rd of March, 1993, did you order the arrest of Ferdo Gazibaric for these events?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I demanded of the assistant for security that a complete investigation be undertaken on the events, what Zuti had done and what his group had done and, once again, that Ferdo Gazibaric be returned to prison, but the incident was a major incident and there were some problems because it was an incident within the military police itself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Nothing happened either to Ferdo Gazibaric or to Zarko Andric, also known as Zuti, or to any members of the Vitezovi, or to any members of Tvrtko II for this breaking out of Ferdo Gazibaric from prison; isn't that right? Nothing happened?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: That is not correct. That is not correct. Mr. Ferdo Gazibaric, after a certain amount of time, committed another criminal act. Then, with remuneration, monetary remuneration, and with the help of the members of the BH army, he fled to south-western Herzegovina. He escaped there. When I received authorisation of direct authority over the military police, I asked that the commander of the military police dispatch a writ for him to be returned, which was dispatched to Mostar and Gazibaric, and he was arrested. He was returned on the basis of this warrant. He was taken to the military district prison and tried at the military district court in Vitez. Furthermore, measures were taken against the other members who had taken part in these activities in November 1993. When an attempt was made to arrest them, there was an armed conflict between the members of the military police and the members of this criminal group, and eight to ten of them were arrested and put into prison, the district prison, and they were prosecuted at the military district court in Vitez. So these members were prosecuted and one of them lost their life in this shoot-out with the military police. A military police member was also wounded in this settling of accounts with the group that called itself the Zuti group or whatever else they chose to call themselves.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, this event that took place between the 26th and -- between the 27th of February, 1993 and the time when Zuti was shot and essentially paralysed on the 22nd of October of 1993, did you arrest Zuti for this outrageous act?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Zuti, at the time you're asking me about, was a member of the military police, so I had no authority to even issue a disciplinary measure, let alone detain a member of the military police. This was not under my competencies. It was under the competency and the authority of the military police. So I wasn't able to give a disciplinary measure to the members of the military police. He was within the military police of the 4th Battalion, and Mr. Pasko Ljubicic was his superior. But I requested that an investigation be conducted, and I asked the security service, in addition to this material, the assistant SIS individual investigate it within the military police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The bottom line, General, is that Zuti was not arrested between the 27th or the 28th of February and the 22nd of October, 1993 when he was shot; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, he was not arrested, as far as I know, but I did not have information as to what the military police undertook against him, what measures they took against him, because when he perpetrated this incident, he was, as I say, a member of the military police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us turn our attention to Prosecutor's Exhibit 97. If we can highlight 97 and the other exhibits that I gave you a list of, please. It does note in 213 of this report, does it not, that: "From the rooms of the 4th Military Police Battalion, communication was established with Colonel Blaskic in Kiseljak. The situation they found themselves in was described to him, as well as the consequences which could result if their demands were not met and armed conflict occurred. Blaskic's suggestion was to do all this without the use of force and without bloodshed." Now, you were the one that was making the decisions on how the military police was going to conduct themselves in this matter, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Let me clarify here, Your Honours. The members of the military police attacked the command of the military police, the military police headquarters, and it was a settling of accounts within the military police because the military police had arrested a criminal and placed him in the district prison. When the military police was completely disarmed and the commander of the military police found himself in front of his subordinate disarmed, he called me and informed me that he had been completely disarmed and that they threatened to liquidate him unless this particular criminal, Gazibaric, were freed from the prison, the district prison. I then wanted to contact the chief of that particular band, group of men, and told him not to free the prisoner by force, that this was illegal, against the law, and that he must be conscious of all the consequences of acting in that way were he to opt to do so. He told me over the telephone, he said, "Okay." Now, this "all right," I understood this to mean that he would not undertake the next step, that is to say, to attack the district prison and free the prisoner by force. Despite saying "all right" to me and despite agreeing with my position, he went to the district prison and forcefully freed the prisoner. The individual writing the report did not hear my conversation, the conversation that I had by telephone. It was an ordinary civilian telephone that I used for the conversation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the third-to-last paragraph of that document, Ljubicic notes: "I received on time the information about the intentions of this group to free Gazibaric by means of firearms, and at the same time I warned about what would happen, so that there were many possibilities to organise the military police units and to prevent this group on time in their intentions." Now, on routine police matters, the military police was under your command. While operating as such, did Pasko Ljubicic warn you what was going to happen?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Pasko Ljubicic, in that situation, was directly subordinate to the military police command according to the regulations on the organisation of the military police and according to explanations given to me by the officer of the military police in the presence of General Petkovic at a meeting on the 13th of December, 1992. Pasko Ljubicic called me up on the 27th of February, 1993 when the attack had already been completed and when he had been disarmed. So this group here, it transpired, was connected to other groups and was far stronger than the military police at the time, both with regard to their arms, the weapons they had. They had tanks within their composition, guns, that is, so it was very difficult to disarm these groups by force. They were strong.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You would agree, General, that this act or crime by Zuti and his members was a very, very serious matter in the Central Bosnia Operative Zone, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Of course it was a serious matter, but the situation in the Central Bosnia Operative Zone was similar when the refugees from Jajce came into conflict with the Croats in Novi Travnik, and I think that this was an incident within the military police, as I say. There were other attacks on the district prison --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Excuse me. I have another question. If we can turn our attention to Prosecutor's 97? In prosecutor's 97, at 3D, this date is May the 11th, "... were two Muslim families in Nova Bila forced out of their houses by a special HVO unit, and two Croat families took over the houses. The commander of the HVO unit had the nickname Zuti or 'Yellow.'" It is signed down at the bottom by Lars Baggesen who was a witness before this Court and another individual, Stavros, and I'm not sure what the pronunciation of that Greek name is. Nevertheless, Mr. Baggesen testified at page 978 about this incident: "Who did you complain to about this incident?" We can move up to the top on 1978 on line 3: "Q Where is Nova Bila? A This is close to Vitez. We went to that area and we witnessed two Muslim families were forced out of their houses, and their houses were given over to Croat families. Q Who forced them out of their houses? A It was an HVO unit, we were able to see that, and we were told the commander of this HVO unit had the nickname Zuti. We heard this name on other occasions as well." Line 22 of 1978: "Q Who did you complain to about this incident? A On our way back, we passed Colonel Blaskic, and we complained about this to Colonel Blaskic. Q You said you passed Colonel Blaskic. You passed the Hotel Vitez and you went into his headquarters and you told him about the incident? What did he say? A He said he was sorry and he would try to do something about it." What did you do about it, General?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, I asked that all information be sent to me on this incident and who the perpetrators were who had expelled the Bosniak Muslim families. I can't remember the names and everything else at the moment. But in cases of that kind, I would have talks with those who were expelled and ask the military police to ensure their return. I have jotted down some of the names that I found in my notes and records, but I can't remember the specifics of each individual case at this point in time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you order the military police to arrest Zuti for expelling Bosnian Muslims from their homes, after you had written all these orders prohibiting that? Did you do that? If you did, when?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I issued an order to the military police to arrest all the members of those criminal groups who referred to Zuti, and that was sometime at the end of October and beginning of November 1993, when I succeeded in organising and forming and capacitating the military police. I was not in a position to issue and command the military police until July 1993 because the military police was subordinate to the military police head office. I just had the right to issue them daily operative assignments.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, information was brought to your attention on the 11th of May, 1993 about a military policeman in your zone of operations committing crimes against Muslims. Did you go to the district military prosecutor and refer that information that Mr. Baggesen had given to you so that Zuti could be arrested and prosecuted?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: If information arrived that the members of the HVO had committed a certain offence, then that information -- what I did was I would ask the assistant for security to check the whole matter, to investigate the case, and then to file a criminal report with the district military court. The military police had a crime department within its composition who also had the task of filing criminal reports with the military district court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe? General, Mr. Kehoe asked you this question: "Did you go to the district military prosecutor and refer that information that Mr. Baggesen had given to you so that Zuti could be arrested and prosecuted?" Would you mind telling me what is your answer to that question? Did you go to the district military prosecutor, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Your Honour, I do not recall how Major Baggesen formulated his assertion. Did he say they were members of the HVO or did he say in concrete terms that they were members of the HVO and the Zuti group? But if I did receive a complaint that individual members of the HVO had done something wrong, then I would ask the assistant for security to check it out, to check out the information, and then to send in a written report to me on what really took place. If they were the members of the HVO and the home guard units, then a criminal report would be filed with the military district court. I have a case dated the 27th of May, and it was a case of Nesib Ahmic who was thrown out of his home and who was returned later on with assurances from the military police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Do I understand your position to be this, that you did not regard the information which Mr. Baggesen gave you as sufficiently concrete for you to refer to the military court?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: If Mr. Baggesen informed me that the members of the HVO did that without specifying who, I asked the security service to check this out and to get the actual names and surnames so that I could give this information to the military court or, rather, the military prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: But you didn't have information of that kind to enable you to refer the matter to the military prosecutor; is that it? I'm trying to understand you.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: When Major Baggesen gave me this information, I can only assume now that he did not give me the names and surnames of the members of the HVO who committed such an offence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, General, certainly you know that the district military prosecutor has the capability and is authorised to conduct investigations himself; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I believe he is authorised, although I'm not a lawyer, to carry out an investigation on this, but I know that members of the civilian and military police would file criminal reports concerning all events to the district prosecutor who would then decide on whether proceedings would be initiated. Then I would receive information on the sum total of criminal reports. During the first three months, there were 92 criminal reports altogether, which is a lot for that area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, based on the event of the 11th of May, 1993 where you were informed that Muslims were being expelled from their homes in Nova Bila by members of Zuti's group, did anything happen to either Zuti or to any member of his group as a result of this event?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Measures were taken against all who were expelling people. Already on the 21st of April, I issued an order prohibiting expulsions and asking for security and safety.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm talking about the event of the 11th of May, 1993 that was brought to your attention by Major Baggesen concerning the expulsion of Muslims from Nova Bila by Zuti and his members. Did anything happen to Zuti or any of his members as a result of that crime that you were put on notice of?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: At this moment, I do not have individual information here with me on all the disciplinary measures that were taken or the criminal measures that were taken. I had numerous information, but at my level, I did not have information as to names.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, General, let us move to another incident on Zuti where you sent your chief of staff, Franjo Nakic, up to deal with, and that had to do with the theft of General Alagic's automobile by Zuti and Zuti's members; do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Could you tell me which date you're talking about?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The 2nd of June.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I think we're going to take a break. This is going to be a new area that you're getting into. I suggest that we take a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We can now resume the hearing. Please be seated. Mr. Kehoe?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, did you have a chance to look at your chronology, and if you did, do you recall the event where Zuti and his men stole Alagic's property from him?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I did not recall such an event nor did I speak of such an event.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall sending your chief of staff, Franjo Nakic, to meet with Zuti to get Alagic's property back?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I do not recall having spoken about that. If you have it somewhere. I did speak about the incident with the commander of the Operative Group of Bosanska Krajina, Alagic, on the 2nd of June, 1993 but and not in that context and not about that event.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In that context, did Zuti and his men take Alagic's property?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Your Honours, perhaps the interpretation is not proper. The question was whether Zuti and his men take away Alagic's property. They did not. The members of Zuti did not have an incident on the 2nd of June, 1993 with General Alagic. It was this way: Commander Alagic was stopped and provoked by the members of the Travnik Brigade of the HVO. If that is the incident that you're referring to. I sent two officers, Mr. Jazbinski and Mr. Lovrenovic, with a letter of apology and they were supposed to report to Mr. Alagic with that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us turn our attention to yet another order of yours, General, and we'll look at 456/37. I'm interested in the English version that was signed by the General.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me. There is an English version that is signed by the General. That is the translation. There is an English version that is signed by the witness. If we can go up just a little further on that. Up the other way, Mr. Usher.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, General, this was an order that was signed by you on the 19th of June, 1993, and in number 3 it notes, among other things that: "Every stealing and holding of property shall be punished and solved through the military discipline measures and courts." The distribution, in the lower left-hand corner, is to all the HVO brigades and all the independent units under the command of the HVO 3rd Operative Zone commander, MTD, 4th LTRD, the 4th Military Police Battalion, the Vitezovi, Tvrtko II, and Zuti. Now, this is signed by you, isn't it, General?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You describe these units, the 4th Military Police Battalion, Vitezovi, Tvrtko II, and Zuti as being under your command; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President, regrettably, once again the interpreters are putting in words, key words, that do not exist here and they work to the detriment of our client. I thought that this was -- at first I thought it was an accident but now I see it is not. Look at this translation first. In the bottom left corner --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me, counsel. Before you make accusations, let us make sure that we are talking about the document that is signed by the accused. It is an English document signed by the accused that is part of 456/37. In the lower left-hand corner, in English, in the English version that the witness signed, it notes: "All the independent units under the command of the HVO, 3rd Operative Zone Commander."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We're talking about an English document here.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Perhaps I have been misunderstood. I'm not talking about the translation and interpretation unit of this court, I'm talking about Blaskic's people. I suggest that the original text in Croatian be put on the ELMO, the one that Blaskic could have read, and then you will see that it does not say: "All the independent units under the command of the HVO, the Commander of the 3rd Operative Zone," but it says --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me, counsel. Mr. President, this is a matter for redirect examination if counsel so chooses to bring this matter up in redirect examination. This is an exhibit that was signed by the accused where the witness makes representations to the International Community that these units are under his command. Now, if counsel wants to talk about this in redirect, he's certainly free to do so, I would suspect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: General Blaskic has to answer. Let me remind you once again that your client chose to become a witness and he has to be allowed to testify as he wants to. You will always be in a position to reply. It does seem that this is a document in English which is signed by General Blaskic, who at the time was a Colonel, Colonel Blaskic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, but under the same number you have the document in the Croatian language and it is identical except for this part where it says that these are units under the command of General Blaskic. That's what I'm talking about. It is the same number, 38. There is the Croatian version that Blaskic understood and read. He doesn't understand the English version. I'm just showing this significant difference. At first I thought that this was a mistake in the interpretation here, but then after a few seconds I saw that this was a mistake in translation at Mr. Blaskic's office, but in this case we have the Croatian original.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right. You can develop that in your redirect. Perhaps Colonel Blaskic should also have asked for disciplinary measures for his translators at the time, but for now I would like the Prosecutor to be able to ask the questions he wants of General Blaskic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, in a document that you signed to the International Community, you noted that these units, the 4th Military Police Battalion, Vitezovi, Tvrtko II, and Zuti were under your command, the command of the 3rd Operative Zone commander, which was you; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I have the document that you're talking about here, 456/37, in the Croatian language and it is quite clear. Unfortunately, at that time, I really did not know a word of English and I did not understand either. I did not mean to say that all --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: What's in the Croatian language? Let's not spend any more time on this. What does it say in Croatian? Can we see it on the ELMO, and let's have the interpreters interpret it for us. Let's move forward. I think we're getting a little bit lost this afternoon. All right. Mr. Usher, would you give me the French version, please? We have the version in Croatian. Would you give the Judges the English version, please? I have it in French. It says: "To all brigades." Could I ask the interpreters to translate the addressees of the document, that is, for Judge Shahabuddeen and for Judge Rodrigues, both the English and in French. I would like the Croatian version to be put on the ELMO and that it be translated in respect of the most important point, that is, the addressees. Mr. Nobilo, would you read it out, please? Don't you have it? Mr. Kehoe, yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I note that the witness sent out two versions, a version in B/C/S that he signed and a version in English that he signed at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, but the witness has the right to point out that perhaps this was not exactly the correct translation even if his defenders can do it during their redirect. So that we don't waste too much time let's try to throw light on the problem immediately. I ask, in respect of what is on the ELMO, whether the Judges can have the translation first of the document that's on the ELMO. I have the impression, in respect to the French version, that it's addressed to all brigades. What does it say? Let's continue. "To all brigades and autonomous units"; is that right? Yes, go ahead. Please translate the rest.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Perhaps I can read it out. It says: "To all brigades and independent units." Then the next line says, "MTD, LARD, the 4th Battalion of the Military Police, Logistics Base Stojkovici, PPN Vitezovi, Tvrtko II, and Zuti" and nowhere does it say, "Under my command."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: So there are two documents that were issued on the same day. I'm going to ask the -- have the Prosecutor ask the witness were there two documents. Do you have an explanation? Was the addressee indicated on the -- perhaps it means the same thing. I have the impression that the version you're referring to, Mr. Nobilo, talks about the distribution here, which is exactly the same. Could we bring it back up? For example, in the present version, on the left lower corner it says, "Made in three copies." Perhaps that is the only difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: But it also says, "Copies to," one to those whom it was addressed to, one to the operative teaching department, and one to archives, but these are two identical orders. Only this part is different in terms of who copies are sent to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Could we say that in the document that you were referring to, and the Judges thank you for having called their attention to this point, could one consider that when the Prosecutor says, "To all brigades and independent units" in one the version, that is the English version, in actuality, in the version that you're alluding to, "All of the brigades" is at the bottom on the left side; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: In the Croatian version, in the top right-hand corner it says who all the addressees are, that is to say, all brigades, independent units, et cetera, whereas in the English text, the addressees are in the left-hand bottom corner. However, the significant difference is that in the English text it says that it is sent to special purpose units that are under the command of the commander of the Operative Zone. That does not exist in the Croatian language, the one that Blaskic understood then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Nobilo. All right. Mr. Kehoe, please ask your questions, because we know that there is this slight problem here. Mr. Kehoe?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, did you inform the International Community that Zuti, this independent unit, was under your command?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: All special purpose units were under the command of my superiors, that is to say, the head of the defence department, the head of the security service. If I had a conversation -- I do not recall having had a conversation with representatives of the International Community about the structure. Perhaps I talked about that too but, specifically, I do not recall whether we had a conversation, because these documents, 456/37, pertain to agreements on a ceasefire in June 1993, but these special purpose units under my direct command, no, they were never under my direct command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us move on, General. Now, after the military police commander became Mr. Marinko Palavra in early August 1993, you mentioned to him in a conversation, and I note on page 16752 of Mr. Palavra's testimony, that there were criminal elements not only within the military police but also the Vitezovi and the Zuti. So as of August when Mr. Palavra took over, there continued to be criminals within the Zuti unit; correct?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: There were persons with a criminal record, but the greatest problem was to identify the perpetrators of these crimes. That was the major problem that the military police had in this area after Palavra became commander.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When Captain Whitworth testified on page 10361 at line 11 that "Zuti seemed to have an endless supply of weapons," was that also true?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know what kind of a supply of weapons you are referring to that was under his control. I know that Captain Whitworth was the organiser of the meeting between Mr. Asim Fazlic, that is to say, to buy explosives for the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Zuti was a merchant and he traded with Bosniak Muslims, and he had very good trade relations with them, especially in view of the black market. But I don't know which context you're placing this, that is, in terms of the arms supplied during a total blockade and isolation of this area, that is to say, Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me turn to the cross-examination questions by Mr. Hayman of Mr. Whitworth concerning Grbavica, and the question on page 10419 was: "Q Did Zuti come with a group of men to loot and scavenge?" We're talking about after the Grbavica attack. His answer is: "A I don't recall seeing Zuti. Q Zuti was from Nova Bila; correct? A Nova Bila, Novi Travnik, yes. Q How do you recall that people came from Nova Bila specifically if you didn't see Zuti or some indication of Zuti's men? A There were a lot of people in Nova Bila than there were Zuti, and there were numerous flatbed trucks, and I knew a lot of people in Nova Bila whom I dealt with when doing the evacuations and could identify items and trucks that I had seen in the vicinity during the looting." Now, General, was Zuti involved in the looting in Grbavica?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I am not aware of his participation, and I imagine that the witness, Lee Whitworth, replaced this by the Tvrtko unit from Nova Bila. They did take part in the Grbavica operation because they came from the same area, and they did take part, but they did not loot Grbavica. Grbavica was looted by refugees, mostly refugees from the municipalities of Travnik and Zenica. The civilian police killed one of the refugees during looting, but they were not in the position to stop further looting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To your knowledge, you don't know if Zuti and his men were involved in looting or not; is that right?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I do not have any information as to their participation. I did not receive any information to that effect, whether there were such individuals. I really do not recall having received such information.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, General, Zuti was shot and paralysed in a gun battle between criminal groups on the 22nd of October, 1993; is that right?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, this was a conflict in Novi Travnik, and he was paralysed, and that is true, yes, that he remained paralysed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That took place on the 22nd of October, I think you told us, 1993?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I can check the exact date if it's important, but it was around that date that this incident occurred, in October 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, General, let me just refresh your recollection about an incident and time, and you told us that on the 30th of April, 1993 that Brigadier Petkovic came to Vitez and gave a speech to you and your staff. On page 19082 at line 13, he noted: "... the town is full of snipers, gangs, and the ordinary men in the street is tired of all of this and they've had enough of all of this, and they're waiting for this to be over. So take all measures to control these groups in the area." Now, one of the criminal groups that he is talking about there is Zuti and his group; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Let me just have a look, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The 30th of April, 1993.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I think that this context is related to what Brigadier Petkovic or, rather, General Petkovic said, and this was in relation to the general situation in the town of Vitez. When he talked about snipers in the town and that area, he was referring to the snipers that were operating from Stari Vitez and individuals from the HVO. However, he did not refer to the criminal group of Zuti because they operated in the territory of the municipality of Travnik, that is to say, a completely different area. So that's not the way I understood him, nor is that the way he emphasised it in his statement, that is to say, he did not specifically highlight that criminal group or another criminal group.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So is your testimony, General, so I understand you correctly, is it your testimony that when Petkovic noted, and I quote what you said: "He said the town is full of snipers, gangs, and the ordinary men in the street is tired of all this, and they've had enough of all this and they're waiting for this to be over. So take all measures to control these groups in this area, and they should not act as they wish to. Civilians have to be defended. Chaos is a folly for all. Let the military police arrest individuals." Now, the criminal groups that Petkovic is telling you and these others that must be suppressed, do those criminal groups include Zuti and his men or not?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: When Petkovic spoke about this matter, I believe he had in mind the town of Vitez because the meeting was held in Vitez, whereas Zuti and his group were active in the Travnik municipality area, that is, a neighbouring municipality, neighbouring on Vitez. Whether General Petkovic had that group in mind or not, I did not have a chance to exchange opinions as to that. I just believe that he was talking about the situation in Vitez because he held the meeting in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Had you told General Petkovic, in all these communiqués that you had back and forth, about the problems you had with people like Zuti? Had you told him that?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know what contacts you mean. I informed General Petkovic of all the more important events and formations in the Operative Zone area. At that time, we discussed the war crime that occurred in Ahmici mostly, that is to say, prior to the meeting that General Petkovic held with my command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you tell him in all of the reports that you sent to him about the problem with this fellow Zuti and his band of thieves? Did you ever tell him anything about that?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I informed General Petkovic about all the groups that were active in the region; however, Zuti as an individual could not be recognised in the region by criminal groups or criminal acts, but criminal groups would use his name. He personally engaged in trade, and with the Bosniak Muslims, he had communications throughout and relationships with them throughout. So it was not he himself that manifested activities of this kind but groups who would use his name. Except on the 27th of February, he didn't take part in any of the events, and he was a member of the military police at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, General, we're talking about the same man who broke prisoners out of the Kaonik gaol, aren't we? I mean, Zuti is the same man, isn't he?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, we're talking about the same man, but something else is being created here. He did not have the same function. When he broke out the prisoners, he was commander of the company, and it was an armed uprising. So he was the commander of the company of a military police company, and he stood up against the command of the battalion because one of the soldiers or sympathisers were placed in prison by the commander of the battalion. So this was an incident and a settling of accounts within the military police which is subordinate to the head office of the military police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The bottom line, General, is that when he did that, that was a very, very serious crime, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: When he did that within the military police, of course, it was a serious crime, but for that crime, it was the head office of the military police that was responsible, that is to say, within the institution of the military police. That is where a crime had taken place, perpetrated by the commander of a company against the commander of a battalion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, let me refer you to your typed-out chronology, and take a look at the 4th of July, 1993. While you're doing that, I'll read to you what you said on page 19406, your --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Let the witness go back to his own chronology, and then you can say what you want. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes. I apologise, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: You said the 4th of July, 1993, did you?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I've looked at my chronology.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me read to you, General, what you testified to this Court: "A On the 4th of July, 1993, I received information from the Military Intelligence Service that the BH army was grouping significant forces in the village of Zivcici which was in the Fojnica municipality and that it was bearing forces for offensive operations, probably in the direction of Fojnica, and from the security service, I was informed that three members of the Vitezovi had committed suicide while on duty with that unit." Do you have any information in your chronology about Zuti, Zarko Andric?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I do not for that day. I have no information for that day, and that corresponds to what I said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me show you an order, General.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is Prosecution Exhibit 685, 685A for the English version.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There is no French copy of this, General, so we will read this. Firstly, is that your signature, General?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, that is my signature.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that your stamp?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, that is the stamp of the Central Bosnia Operative Zone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us read this, dated 4 July, 1993, on HVO letterhead. "Pursuant to provisions of Article 34, paragraph 2 of the Decree on the OS /Armed Forces/ of the HVO /Croatian Defence Council/ of the HZ HB /Community of Herceg-Bosna/ - Final Version, and the approval given by the Supreme Commander of the OS HVO HZ HB, number 396/2 of 27 June 1992, the Commander of the OZ SB, hereby Appoints to the OZ SB Command: 1. Mr. Zarko Andric as Assistant Commander for the Active Forces of the OZ SB. 2. This appointment and establishment post are temporary and valid until further notice. Signed, Commander Tihomir Blaskic." Now, General, this man who your counsel has described as a Mafioso boss and that you have described as a criminal, you appoint as the assistant commander for the active forces for the Central Bosnia Operative Zone on the 4th of July, 1993, don't you?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, that is true, and I did so to pacify him and to place him under any kind of control. At that time, for a military settling of accounts for him in any way there wasn't the power to do so, and he became assistant commander for the active forces which, in fact, did not exist in the Central Bosnia Operative Zone. We were only to create forces of that kind. After that, there were no major incidents after this appointment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Except the fact that there was the shoot-out in October where one boss was shot and killed and Zuti was shot and paralysed; is that right?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Nobody was killed. The shoot-out did not take place in that way. There was a settling of account between two commanders. On the one hand there was Zuti and on the other there was a commander called Tuka, and Zuti was wounded. Several days after that, there was -- a killing took place perpetrated by his sympathisers, Zuti's sympathisers in Vitez. So that the settling of accounts was not between two criminals. Commander Tuka was commander in the Travnik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, General, is this your idea of ensuring that criminals are removed from the HVO and don't have any influence in the HVO? Is this your idea of how to bring that out, by making Zuti a commander within the Hotel Vitez?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: That was not my idea. Zuti was never commander at the Vitez Hotel. From this order you can see that he is assistant for the active forces. At that time, in the Central Bosnia Operative Zone, there was not a single active unit. So professional units began with the formation of a 3rd Guards Brigade on the 15th of January, 1994. Zuti performed his function in a training centre in Nova Bila, and that is where he was in charge of the training of recruits. He helped logistically and so on. That was the only possible way at that time of placing him under any form of control whatsoever, because the military police did not have the strength to settle accounts with him at the time when we were under total encirclement.
